outcome: No resolution and no verified counterexample of the Vaught conjecture appeared between 26 January 2024 and 13 October 2026. The window holds several partial results that confirm the conjecture for restricted classes of theories (Moconja–Tanović 2024 and 2026; Kurilić 2026 on partial orders and on unions of products of rooted trees), one structural paper constraining any hypothetical counterexample (Gonzalez–Rossegger–Turetsky, 13 June 2026), and one minimal-counterexample paper that states it proves nothing bearing on the conjecture (Mahmoud, 15 August 2026). Knight's 2002 counterexample claim remains unverified, and no source I found reports it as verified or refuted.
problem_asks: For every complete first-order theory T in a countable language, the number I(T,ℵ0) of countable models of T up to isomorphism is either finite, or ℵ0, or 2^ℵ0. Unpacked: (a) the claim is universal over all such T, not over a class; (b) finite values are allowed; (c) exactly ℵ0 is allowed; (d) exactly 2^ℵ0 is allowed; (e) every other value is excluded, including every uncountable value strictly below 2^ℵ0. Under CH, 2^ℵ0 = ℵ1, so the content lies in ZFC without CH, and the Wikipedia lead identifies the open case as a theory with exactly ℵ1 countable models when the continuum hypothesis fails. The statement does not say which models (or which equivalence) counts, so the isomorphism-type reading is taken as the one the Wikipedia lead gives.

events.what_happened: Morley's theorem on the number of countable models: for a complete countable theory the number of countable models is finite, ℵ0, ℵ1 or 2^ℵ0 (Wikipedia lead, opened). Published in the Journal of Symbolic Logic in 1970 under the title 'The number of countable models'. The year comes from a secondary search summary; the paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Restricts the possible values of I(T,ℵ0) to finite, ℵ0, ℵ1 or 2^ℵ0. This settles the conjecture for every value except exactly ℵ1, which is excluded only when CH holds, per the Wikipedia lead.
events.remains: The case of exactly ℵ1 countable models when 2^ℵ0 > ℵ1 (Wikipedia calls this the open case). The rest of problem_asks is not touched by this event.
events.direction: Partial. Constrains the possible values, and cuts toward the conjecture: the only excluded-but-unresolved value is ℵ1 without CH.

events.what_happened: Proof of Vaught's conjecture for ω-stable theories, cited by Wikipedia as Harrington, Makkai and Shelah (1984), Israel Journal of Mathematics 49(1–3), 259–280, titled 'A proof of Vaught's conjecture for ω-stable theories'. A search summary also attributes a 1981 Shelah theorem covering ω-stable theories (I(T,ℵ0) > ℵ0 implies 2^ℵ0); the year is therefore uncertain between 1981 and 1984. The paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for all complete countable ω-stable theories. This is a restricted class (ω-stable), not the general statement.
events.remains: All complete countable theories outside the ω-stable class, which is the bulk of problem_asks.
events.direction: Partial, confirming. Cuts toward the conjecture for one class.

events.what_happened: Rubin's sharp form of the conjecture for complete theories of linear orders: I(T,ω) lies in {0, 1, 𝔠} (stated in Kurilić's arXiv abstract 2212.13947, opened, and in an Encyclopedia of Mathematics search snippet, which was not opened). Year 1973 comes from the same secondary sources.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for complete theories of linear orders (a restricted class).
events.remains: All theories outside linear orders.

events.what_happened: Confirmation of the conjecture for o-minimal theories, attributed to Mayer (1988) in a search snippet of the Encyclopedia of Mathematics entry (not opened). Also listed in the Wikipedia-linked summaries as a confirmed class.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for o-minimal theories (restricted class).
events.remains: All theories outside the o-minimal class.

events.what_happened: Confirmation for differentially closed fields of characteristic zero (DCF0): there are 2^ℵ0 countable models. Marker's 2007 paper 'The number of countable differentially closed fields' (Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 48(1)) is the published record, per a search result; the Hrushovski–Sokolović argument itself is described in Pillay–Tanović (2025) as unpublished. Neither was opened.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for DCF0 (one theory, which has continuum many countable models). Restricted to one theory.
events.remains: Every other theory.
events.doubts: The Hrushovski–Sokolović argument is recorded by Pillay–Tanović (2025) as unpublished, so the first public written argument may predate 2007 and cannot be dated from what I read. Dated here to the published record.

events.what_happened: Montalbán, 'A computability theoretic equivalent to Vaught's conjecture', arXiv:1206.5682 (first submitted 25 June 2012; v2 6 June 2013). For every L(ω1,ω) theory T, T has fewer than 2^ℵ0 countable models if and only if a computability condition holds on a cone of Turing degrees. The paper also describes the Turing-degree spectra of a hypothetical counterexample's models.
events.delivers: An equivalence reformulating the conjecture in infinitary logic L(ω1,ω) in computability terms. It settles nothing directly and is not a proof for any class.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks. The author presents the result as an equivalent reformulation, not a resolution.
events.direction: Reformulation; neither cuts for nor against the conjecture. It is the infinitary form, which is a different statement from the first-order one in the bullet.

events.what_happened: Assem, 'Distinguishing models by formulas and the number of countable models', arXiv:1301.0994 (v1 6 Jan 2013; v2 24 Apr 2013). Without CH: if a countable-language first-order theory has an uncountable set of pairwise distinguishable countable models, it has such a set of size continuum. The abstract also says the conjecture holds for languages with one unary relation symbol.
events.delivers: Without CH, a partial dichotomy: an uncountable set of pairwise distinguishable countable models forces a set of size continuum. Also confirms the conjecture for the restricted class of theories in a language with one unary relation symbol.
events.remains: The general conjecture, and the ℵ1 case of theories whose countable models are not pairwise distinguishable.
events.direction: Partial. Cuts toward the conjecture for one class and gives a ZFC dichotomy for distinguishable models.

events.what_happened: Kurilić, 'Vaught's conjecture for monomorphic theories', arXiv:1811.07210 (v1 17 Nov 2018; v2 6 Dec 2018). A complete theory with infinite models is monomorphic iff it has a countable monomorphic model; for monomorphic theories I(T,ω) is 1 or 𝔠. Journal version per search: Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 170(8), 2019.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for monomorphic theories (a restricted class, relational signature).
events.remains: Theories outside the monomorphic class.

events.what_happened: Kurilić, 'Vaught's conjecture for almost chainable theories', arXiv:1905.05531 (single version, 14 May 2019). An almost chainable theory has one or continuum many countable models. Journal version per search: J. Symbolic Logic 86(3), 2021, 991–1005.
events.revisions: single version, 14 May 2019 (journal version 2021 per search).
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for almost chainable theories (bounded profile class).
events.remains: Theories with unbounded profile and all others.

events.what_happened: Kurilić, 'Sharp Vaught's conjecture for some classes of partial orders', arXiv:2212.13947 (v1 28 Dec 2022; v2 13 Sep 2023). Proves the sharp form I(T,ω) in {0,1,𝔠} for complete theories of partial orders having a model in the smallest class containing linear orders and closed under finite products and finite disjoint unions; also for an extension of rooted trees with a finite monomorphic decomposition, and for infinite disjoint unions of linear orders. Journal version per search: Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 175(4), 2024.
events.revisions: v1 28 Dec 2022; v2 13 Sep 2023; journal version 2024 per search.
events.delivers: Sharp form of the conjecture for the listed classes of partial orders and trees. These are restricted classes, and the abstract does not claim the general conjecture.
events.remains: All theories outside the listed classes.

events.what_happened: Becker, 'The topological Vaught's conjecture and minimal counterexamples', J. Symbolic Logic 59(3) (1994), 757–784. Works with Borel actions of Polish groups; the topological conjecture implies the model-theoretic one for L(ω1,ω). Existence of minimal counterexamples to the topological version is proved there, per a search summary. Not opened.
events.delivers: A stronger topological statement that implies the infinitary model-theoretic version. It is a stronger conjecture, not a case of this one, and it settles nothing.
events.remains: The conjecture itself.
events.direction: Neither confirms nor refutes. Reduces the model-theoretic statement to a topological one.

events.what_happened: Robin Knight announced a counterexample to the Vaught conjecture and to the topological Vaught conjecture. The first draft (May 2002) is a 117-page .ps file on Knight's Oxford preprints page; the page itself says 'The example is unstable.' An expanded informal description was posted 3 January 2003. Knight's page also lists a second draft and corrections, and a simplified four-part version whose Part 4 (the one that constructs a 'Vaughtian Stack') is listed as forthcoming and 'not yet available'. Wikipedia (revised June 2025) says the counterexample 'has not been verified' as of 2021.
events.revisions: first draft May 2002; expanded informal description 3 Jan 2003; second draft and corrections undated; simplified four-part version undated, Part 4 forthcoming.
events.delivers: Claims a counterexample, meaning a theory with more than ℵ0 but fewer than 2^ℵ0 countable models, to the first-order conjecture and to the topological conjecture. The page says Part 3 reduces the infinitary conjecture for Lω1,ω to constructing a 'Vaughtian Stack', and Part 4 with that construction is not available. As the page stands, the claim is not verified and the construction is not available in full.
events.remains: Nothing is settled by this event as published. Everything in problem_asks is claimed to be violated, but this is unverified.
events.doubts: Author's own page calls the first draft's example 'unstable' and lists further drafts, corrections and a Part 4 not yet available. Wikipedia (2021 status) records it as unverified. A 2025 undergraduate thesis (search summary only, not opened) says the work appears to be no longer available and unverified as of January 2025. No public verification or refutation was found in any source I could open.
events.direction: Cuts against the conjecture if the claim holds: a claimed counterexample. Unverified.
events.object: Knight's claimed construction, not read: a counterexample to the Vaught conjecture in Lω1,ω, built with type categories and partial functions and reduced to a 'Vaughtian Stack' (Part 3 of his page). The page does not say whether the object is explicit or non-constructive. The full text was not available to me.

events.what_happened: Knight, 'Categories of topological spaces and scattered theories', Notre Dame J. Formal Logic 48(1) (2007), 53–77. Per its abstract (as summarised in a search result, not opened in full), it is a framework paper offering a topological treatment of scattered theories, presented as 'a step on the road to fully understanding counterexamples to Vaught's Conjecture', and does not itself announce a counterexample.
events.delivers: Framework and partial theorems toward counterexample analysis. It does not establish a counterexample and does not settle any case.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Neither confirms nor refutes. Background for the 2002 claim.

events.what_happened: Larson, 'Scott processes', arXiv:1407.1920 (submitted 8 July 2014). Gives axioms for Scott processes and uses them to prove, for the infinitary version, Harrington's unpublished 1970s result (a counterexample has models at cofinally many Scott ranks below ω2) and a Harnik–Makkai theorem (a counterexample may be chosen with a model of Scott rank ω1). Infinitary, not first-order.
events.delivers: Constraints on any hypothetical counterexample in the infinitary logic. It does not construct one and does not settle the conjecture.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks.
events.direction: Constrains a hypothetical counterexample. Neither confirms nor refutes.

events.what_happened: Baldwin, Friedman, Koerwien and Laskowski, 'Three red herrings around Vaught's conjecture', Trans. AMS 368(5) (2016). Per search summaries (not opened), it strengthens Hjorth's result: a counterexample, if one exists, can be taken so that every model of cardinality ℵ1 is maximal, and it discusses why several natural strategies do not work.
events.delivers: Constraints on a hypothetical counterexample (infinitary). It names three false leads and does not settle the conjecture.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks.
events.direction: Constrains a hypothetical counterexample. Neither confirms nor refutes.

events.what_happened: Moconja, 'Stationarily ordered types and the number of countable models', arXiv:1804.07231 (2018; published Annals of Pure and Applied Logic 2020 per search). Per a search summary (not opened), it confirms the conjecture for binary, stationarily ordered theories.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for binary stationarily ordered theories (restricted class), per the search summary.
events.remains: Theories outside that class.

events.what_happened: Gonzalez and Montalbán, 'The ω-Vaught's conjecture', arXiv:2211.02156 (submitted 3 November 2022). Introduces the ω-Vaught conjecture, a strengthening of the infinitary Vaught conjecture, and shows infinitary sentences whose models are linear orders satisfy it. The abstract does not say whether it covers the first-order conjecture.
events.delivers: An infinitary analogue (ω-Vaught for L(ω1,ω) sentences with linear-order models). It is a different statement and does not settle the first-order conjecture.
events.remains: The first-order conjecture of this bullet.
events.direction: Neither confirms nor refutes the first-order conjecture: analogue only.

events.what_happened: Tanović, 'Vaught's conjecture for theories of discretely ordered structures', arXiv:2212.13605 (v1 27 Dec 2022; v2 5 Dec 2023; v3 24 Mar 2024). A countable complete first-order theory with a definable infinite discrete linear order has continuum many countable models, by first-order methods. The paper leaves open whether such T is Borel complete. The first public written argument is v1, so the date is 2022, which predates the window; v3 (24 March 2024) falls inside the window.
events.revisions: v1 27 Dec 2022; v2 5 Dec 2023; v3 24 Mar 2024 (current).
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture, in the strong form giving continuum, for theories with a definable infinite discrete linear order. This is a restricted class, and it excludes every countable value.
events.remains: Theories without a definable infinite discrete linear order; Borel completeness of the class is left open by the author.

events.what_happened: Moconja and Tanović, 'Countable models of weakly quasi-o-minimal theories I', arXiv:2412.20589 (v1 29 Dec 2024; v2 21 Feb 2026). Shows every weakly quasi-o-minimal theory that admits a definable shift has 2^ℵ0 countable models. Introduces shifts and triviality of global invariant types. The main theorem's wording is 'I(T,ℵ0)=2^ℵ0'. The paper also says the non-existence of shifts plus failure of two further conditions will suffice to confirm the conjecture and Martin's conjecture for a wide subclass.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for weakly quasi-o-minimal theories with a definable shift (the value is 2^ℵ0). This is a restricted class, and it excludes every countable and finite value for that class.
events.remains: Weakly quasi-o-minimal theories without a definable shift, and every theory outside the weakly quasi-o-minimal class.

events.what_happened: Hongyu Zhu, 'Survey on Vaught's Conjecture', a specialty-exam talk in the UW–Madison Logic Seminar, 8 October 2024, with slides at web.math.wisc.edu/logic/talks/241008-Zhu.pdf. Covers alternative formulations, known results and the ω-stable case. Slides not opened beyond a search snippet.
events.delivers: Expository. Establishes no new result.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Gonzalez, Harrison-Trainor and Ho, 'Scott analysis, linear orders and almost periodic functions', arXiv:2406.01836 (3 June 2024). Constructs, for every limit ordinal λ, a linear order of Scott complexity Σ_{λ+1}. Vaught's conjecture appears only as background (linear orders are 'one of the known examples in which Vaught's conjecture holds', citing Steel 1978). The paper does not prove or extend the conjecture.
events.delivers: Nothing about the conjecture. It is about Scott complexity of linear orders. Recorded as a discarded neighbouring event.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: None. Discarded: not about the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Pillay and Tanović, 'The number of countable models of first-order theories', arXiv:2508.06854 (v1 9 Aug 2025; v2 15 Aug 2026). Expository survey on Vaught's conjecture, Martin's conjecture and Ehrenfeucht theories, submitted to the Journal of Open Mathematical Problems. States 'Vaught's conjecture is widely open in both directions.' Reports unpublished claims: Pillay has an unpublished proof for a narrow class (regular, non-connected-by-finite abelian groups in locally modular theories whose nongeneric part is ω-stable, by adapting ideas from the weakly minimal case); Saffe's unpublished work whose proposition was later found to contain a mistake; and Hrushovski–Sokolović's unpublished result for DCF0. No new theorem is claimed.
events.delivers: Nothing new. It reports unpublished claims, one of them for a narrow class of modules, and states the conjecture is open.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: The Pillay claim is unpublished and is stated only inside the survey. Saffe's proposition is described as containing a mistake. Both are recorded in disputes, not as results.

events.what_happened: Moconja, talk at the Beijing International Center for Mathematical Research, scheduled 16 October 2025, 'Around Vaught's conjecture for weakly o-minimal theories', surveying confirmations for some weakly o-minimal theories. Per the BICMR listing (search snippet, not opened), only a partial answer is known in that setting.
events.delivers: Expository talk on partial answers. Establishes no new result.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Montalbán, Chapter 12 'Vaught's conjecture' of Computable Structure Theory: Beyond the Arithmetic (Cambridge University Press, 2026), published online 30 January 2026, pp. 199–208, DOI 10.1017/9781108780568.013. Per the publisher's summary (search snippet, not opened), it is mostly expository and does not contain fully detailed proofs.
events.delivers: Expository. Restates the 2012–2013 computability reformulation and summarises what is known. No new theorem is claimed in the publisher summary.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Kurilić, 'Vaught's conjecture and theories of partial order admitting a finite lexicographic decomposition', arXiv:2601.03155 (single version, 6 January 2026). For complete theories of partial orders with a finite lexicographic decomposition (FLD1 theories): the conjecture holds iff the theory is large or its atomic model has a VC-decomposition; it holds for every 'actually Vaught' FLD1 theory; and the sharp form holds if some model has a VC#-decomposition. The paper says the conjecture is confirmed for a large class of partial orders built from linear orders, Boolean algebras and a broad class of trees.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for FLD1 theories of partial orders in the stated cases, and gives an iff criterion within the class. The restriction is to partial orders with a finite lexicographic decomposition. This does not cover all theories.
events.remains: Partial orders outside FLD1 and all non-order theories.
events.direction: Partial, confirming, for one class. The 'iff' criterion is within the class.

events.what_happened: Moconja and Tanović, 'Countable models of weakly quasi-o-minimal theories II', arXiv:2603.06430 (single version, 6 March 2026). Abstract: 'We confirm Martin's conjecture for a broad subclass of weakly quasi-o-minimal theories.' Theorem 2 (per the body excerpt): Martin's conjecture holds for almost ℵ0-categorical weakly quasi-o-minimal theories. Theorem 1 (per the body excerpt): I(T,ℵ0)=2^ℵ0 if T has no simple semiintervals or has a non-convex 1-type. The introduction calls Martin's conjecture 'a strengthening of Vaught's conjecture'.
events.delivers: Confirms Martin's conjecture, which the authors describe as a strengthening of Vaught's conjecture, for almost ℵ0-categorical weakly quasi-o-minimal theories; and gives 2^ℵ0 for two further sub-classes (Theorem 1 as read). Whether that is a confirmation of Vaught's conjecture for these theories follows from the strengthening relation the authors state, and is for the judging pass to decide. The abstract itself does not claim Vaught's conjecture.
events.remains: Weakly quasi-o-minimal theories outside the sub-classes, and the general conjecture.
events.doubts: Read only up to about 100,000 characters of a 166,000-character page; the proof bodies were not read. The abstract names Martin's conjecture only.
events.direction: Partial, confirming, for sub-classes; Martin's conjecture is stated by the authors as a strengthening of Vaught's.

events.what_happened: Kurilić, 'Vaught's conjecture for unions of products of rooted trees', arXiv:2606.12014 (single version, submitted 10 June 2026). For a finite disjoint union of finite products of rooted trees, the abstract states: 'Vaught's conjecture is true for' the theory, with I(T)=κ if κ ∈ {1, ω, 𝔠} and otherwise I(T) ∈ [3, ω), where κ is the product of the component counts. The paper also gives elementary equivalence, elementary substructure, atomicity and smallness results. The full text read covers about 100,000 of 150,000 characters.
events.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for theories of finite disjoint unions of finite products of rooted trees. The restriction is to that closure class. The stated values are continuum or finite (≥3), with ω-type values excluded in this class except as κ itself.
events.remains: Theories outside that class, which is the bulk of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Single-author preprint with no checking reported in any source I read. A secondary aggregator page (emergentmind, not opened) describes it as removing a restriction from earlier work; I could not confirm that against the paper.

events.what_happened: Gonzalez, Rossegger and Turetsky, 'Scott analysis below the Vaught ordinal', arXiv:2606.15205 (v1 13 June 2026; v2 26 August 2026, whose listed change is 'Added missing assumptions to statements in Section 3'). Main claims from the abstract and introduction: any counterexample to the conjecture must have at least two models of every parameterized Scott rank, improving Sacks; theories with fewer than continuum many models have trivial Scott spectra; ω-Vaught holds for Ehrenfeucht theories (infinitary); Scott complexity is classified for p-groups, trees and Boolean algebras. The introduction says a route to a proof would be a hypothetical counterexample, and that the only thing stopping the proof idea from going through 'is the influence of a few parameters'.
events.revisions: v1 13 Jun 2026; v2 26 Aug 2026 ('Added missing assumptions to statements in Section 3').
events.delivers: Conditional constraints on any counterexample: at least two models of each parameterized Scott rank, and trivial Scott spectra below continuum. Unconditional only for the infinitary ω-Vaught statement for Ehrenfeucht theories. It does not establish the first-order conjecture for any class.
events.remains: The first-order conjecture in full. The authors say the approach would need a strengthening not yet achieved.
events.doubts: The introduction's footnote states that a missing assumption in Lemma 3.2 was pointed out and the assumption is 'crucial', and that the missing assumption 'was discovered by analyzing a prior version of this paper using GPT 5.6 Sol Pro'. v2 added missing assumptions in Section 3, which is consistent with this but the source does not say so explicitly. Lemma 3.2's gap is a correction to a proof, not a new result. The abstract does not mention it.
events.direction: Constrains a hypothetical counterexample; neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture. The authors describe their route as nearly sufficient for a proof by contradiction.
people: Serafim Batzoglou (credited with pointing out the missing assumption)

events.what_happened: Mahmoud, 'ω1-anchored labels in minimal counterexamples to Vaught's conjecture: a per-witness trichotomy and an unconditional stationary dichotomy', arXiv:2608.15044 (single version, 15 August 2026). The paper proves structural results about models of a minimal counterexample φ, conditional on standing hypotheses (H0)–(H3). Its abstract and §1.3 state that it proves nothing bearing on Vaught's conjecture itself, and that 'Neither limb is approached below.'
events.delivers: Structural results about any minimal counterexample. It explicitly does not establish any part of the conjecture: the abstract says 'We prove nothing bearing on Vaught's conjecture itself.'
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: The author's own abstract disclaims any bearing on the conjecture. Read to about 170,000 characters of 181,000; the acknowledgements and any AI statement were not reached.
events.direction: None on the conjecture; the author disclaims it. Structural analysis of a hypothetical counterexample.

events.what_happened: Freitag and Mutchnik, 'A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture', arXiv:2609.00436 (single version, 31 August 2026). Abstract (verbatim): 'Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. This answers a long-standing open question of Hart, Kim and Pillay (1996).' This is a different conjecture in model theory (stable forking in simple theories). It does not mention Vaught's conjecture, countable models or Morley. Recorded only as a discarded neighbouring event, because it is the same field and the same AI system.
events.delivers: Nothing about Vaught's conjecture. A counterexample to the stable forking conjecture, which is a different statement.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Unrefereed preprint. A search summary (aiweekly) reports the authors' statement about human writing of the proofs, and MathWorld reports that independent verification had not been reported as of 7 September 2026; neither was opened.
events.direction: None on Vaught's conjecture. Different conjecture.

systems.name: ChatGPT 5.6
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors' abstract, used to find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. This is a different conjecture from Vaught's and is recorded only as context. It is not AI involvement in this problem.
systems.basis_quote: Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture.

disputes.summary: Knight (May 2002 draft, Jan 2003 informal description) claims a counterexample to the Vaught conjecture and to the topological conjecture. Wikipedia records it as not verified as of 2021. Knight's page calls the first example 'unstable' and lists Part 4 (the Vaughtian Stack construction) as not yet available. No source I opened reports it verified or refuted. Not a priority dispute between named people.

Pillay–Tanović (2025 survey) report an unpublished proof by Pillay for a narrow class of modules (locally modular regular non-connected-by-finite abelian groups with ω-stable nongeneric part). Corrects a search summary I first took to mean 'general superstable theories'; the survey does not say that.
Pillay–Tanović (2025 survey) report that Saffe's unpublished work on the problem claimed a proposition that was later found to contain a mistake. The survey gives no further detail.

Moconja–Tanović (March 2026) describe Martin's conjecture as a strengthening of Vaught's conjecture and confirm it for a subclass. Whether that confirms the Vaught conjecture for those theories follows from the strengthening relation as stated by the authors; the abstract itself names only Martin's conjecture.

summary:
Sources opened: the Wikipedia article (last edited 19 June 2025 per its page), Knight's preprints page, and the arXiv abstract pages for every 2022–2026 paper listed below, with the body text of several 2025–2026 papers read to about the first 100,000 characters (see incomplete). Searches (34 WebSearch calls, listed in search.queries) found no resolution, no verified counterexample and no claim by any source that the conjecture is settled since 26 January 2024. The conjecture is still described as open in every 2025–2026 source read: Pillay–Tanović say it is 'widely open in both directions', and the BICMR and Montalbán sources say the same. The events in the window are partial results on restricted classes: Moconja–Tanović Part I (29 Dec 2024), Moconja–Tanović Part II (6 Mar 2026), Kurilić on FLD1 partial orders (6 Jan 2026), Kurilić on unions of products of rooted trees (10 Jun 2026), and Gonzalez–Rossegger–Turetsky (13 Jun 2026), which constrains a hypothetical counterexample without proving anything. Mahmoud (15 Aug 2026) explicitly states it proves nothing bearing on the conjecture. Restricted-class results are all recorded as partial, because each confirms the conjecture for a class and leaves the general statement open. The earlier history (Morley 1970, Harrington–Makkai–Shelah 1984 for ω-stable, Rubin, Mayer, Assem, Kurilić 2018–2022, Tanović 2022) is recorded as events dated to their first public written argument. Knight's 2002 claimed counterexample is the only claim to have cut against the conjecture, and it has stayed unverified for 24 years.

Close calls. (1) Whether class-by-class confirmations move the quantity the statement names: the statement is universal over all complete countable theories, and each event covers a class, so I have recorded each as 'partial' and left the weighing to the judging pass. (2) The Gonzalez–Rossegger–Turetsky introduction says its results are 'nearly' a proof by contradiction, with 'only… a few parameters' missing. Stated by the authors, it is not a proof, and the Emergentmind summary's wording that the results 'nearly compose into a proof' matches the authors' own wording only in spirit. (3) Martin's conjecture: the 2026 Moconja–Tanović result confirms Martin's conjecture, which they describe as a strengthening of Vaught's. Whether that counts for Vaught's conjecture is for the judging pass. (4) The AI footnote in Gonzalez–Rossegger–Turetsky: GPT 5.6 Sol Pro analysed a prior version of the paper and identified a missing assumption in Lemma 3.2. This is checking of a human proof, not new mathematics, so I have not put it in ai.systems. None_found is false and this summary records it. (5) The Freitag–Mutchnik preprint used ChatGPT 5.6 to find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture. That is a different conjecture in model theory and I have recorded it only as a discarded neighbouring event. It is not AI involvement in Vaught's conjecture.

AI search. Searches covered Vaught with AI, GPT, Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, language model, machine learning, 'AI-assisted', Erdős and Lean terms, the OpenAI Astra announcement of 1 August 2026 (ten topics: sphere packing, codes, non-sofic groups, Connes rigidity, circuit complexity, quantum parallel repetition, closest vector problem, Ehrhart's volume conjecture, multicolour Ramsey numbers, extremal numbers; no model theory listed in secondary coverage), AlphaProof Nexus (combinatorics and number theory coverage; no model theory found), and the formal-conjectures repository (no Vaught entry found in search, repository not browsed). The GPT, the Counterexample Machine paper (arXiv 2608.29595, opened) lists combinatorics, number theory, convexity and analysis, and does not mention Vaught or model theory.

What I could not reach. The Encyclopedia of Mathematics page returned HTTP 502 twice. The Morley 1970 and Harrington–Makkai–Shelah 1984 papers were not opened, so their dates and claims come from Wikipedia and search snippets. The Hrushovski–Sokolović result is recorded to its 2007 published record (Marker), and its unpublished 1992 origin is noted in doubts. Full text was not read for several 2025–2026 papers (see incomplete), so the acknowledgements and any AI statement in those sources remain unverified beyond the parts read.
competing_reading: Read the window as a count of confirmations: Moconja–Tanović (2024, 2026), Kurilić (2026, two papers) each confirm the conjecture for a theory class, and the rooted-trees paper states the conjecture is 'true for' its class. Together with the Scott-analysis paper's 'nearly a proof' (which its authors do not claim as a proof), a reader could say the conjecture has moved substantially in the window. The stronger reading of the statement is that each event covers a class and leaves the universal claim open, so none moves the quantity the statement names in the sense the research question asks for. The Freitag–Mutchnik and Gonzalez–Rossegger–Turetsky AI items could be read as AI contributions to this problem, but the first concerns another conjecture and the second is a proof check.
what_would_settle_it: (1) Full text of arXiv 2608.15044 (acknowledgements and any AI statement, which were not reached); full text of 2606.15205 for Lemma 3.2, to see what v2 changed and whether the GPT 5.6 Sol Pro analysis produced any mathematics beyond identifying the gap; full text of 2606.12014 and 2601.03155 beyond the first 100,000 characters. (2) Knight's Part 4 (the Vaughtian Stack construction) or a referee or expert report on the 2002 draft, which would turn the 2002 claim from unverified to either verified or refuted. (3) Pillay's and Saffe's unpublished work, if published. (4) A published journal record for the 2026 preprints, which would add checked_by entries. (5) A check of the OpenAI Astra primary report and the AlphaProof Nexus paper for any model theory item, since only secondary coverage was read. (6) A search of the google-deepmind/formal-conjectures repository and Mathlib for Vaught or countable-model statements with sorry status.

event.what_happened: Moconja and Tanović, 'Countable models of weakly quasi-o-minimal theories I', arXiv:2412.20589 (v1 29 Dec 2024; v2 21 Feb 2026). Shows every weakly quasi-o-minimal theory that admits a definable shift has 2^ℵ0 countable models. Introduces shifts and triviality of global invariant types. The main theorem's wording is 'I(T,ℵ0)=2^ℵ0'. The paper also says the non-existence of shifts plus failure of two further conditions will suffice to confirm the conjecture and Martin's conjecture for a wide subclass.
event.delivers: Confirms the conjecture for weakly quasi-o-minimal theories with a definable shift (the value is 2^ℵ0). This is a restricted class, and it excludes every countable and finite value for that class.
event.remains: Weakly quasi-o-minimal theories without a definable shift, and every theory outside the weakly quasi-o-minimal class.

events.credibility_reason: Unverified for 24 years; author's own page lists corrections and the key Part 4 construction as not yet available; Wikipedia and the 2025 Pillay–Tanović survey treat the conjecture as open.

events.ai_basis: Using ChatGPT 5.6, we find a counterexample to the stable forking conjecture.

judgement.why: The statement is universal over all complete countable first-order theories, so every class-restricted confirmation (ω-stable, linear orders, o-minimal, weakly quasi-o-minimal subclasses, FLD1 partial orders, unions of products of rooted trees) is a case, confirmed. Morley's theorem is scored a case because it settles the conjecture under CH while leaving the ℵ1-without-CH case open. Moconja–Tanović II is a case because its Theorem 1 gives 2^ℵ0 directly for subclasses and Martin's conjecture is stated as a strengthening. Gonzalez–Rossegger–Turetsky, Mahmoud, Larson and BFKL only constrain hypothetical counterexamples and settle nothing, so none; reformulations and surveys are none; infinitary/topological analogues (Becker, ω-Vaught) are variant. GPT 5.6 Sol Pro in GRT only found a missing assumption, which is checking, so none. Freitag–Mutchnik is about a different conjecture (variant); its own quote credits ChatGPT 5.6 with finding the counterexample, which I scored assisted rather than generated because the abstract does not say the model produced the construction unaided — moot since the event is discarded. Knight 2002 is a pre-snapshot whole-scope claimed counterexample, unreviewed and doubtful.
judgement.doubts: Pre-snapshot journal events marked digested on the basis of journal publication reported in secondary sources; this affects nothing post-snapshot. Freitag–Mutchnik AI role (assisted vs generated) is a close call but irrelevant to this problem. Morley 1970 case-vs-bound is a judgement call.
